values and types.definition: A value is data; its type determines which operations make sense. JavaScript has primitive values and objects.
values and types.example: 3 is a number; '3' is a string; {available:3} is an object.

coercion and strict equality.definition: Coercion converts one type into another. === compares without that conversion; == can convert before comparing.

truthiness.definition: Conditions convert values to true or false. A nonempty string is truthy even when its contents say false.
truthiness.example: Boolean('false') is true; Boolean('') is false.

functions.definition: A function is reusable behavior with parameters, a return value, and possibly side effects.
functions.example: validateQuantity(3) returns a result; it should not change outside state.

control flow.definition: Control flow determines which statements execute and in what order, using branches, loops, and early returns.
control flow.example: Reject an invalid quantity before reserving stock.

arrays and objects.definition: Arrays are ordered collections; objects associate property names with values.
arrays and objects.example: A jobs array contains objects with id and status properties.

destructuring and spread.definition: Destructuring extracts fields; spread copies enumerable properties or expands an iterable. Object spread is shallow.
destructuring and spread.example: {...stock, available:2} creates a new outer object.

Map and Set.definition: Map stores key/value associations; Set stores unique values. They suit lookup and duplicate detection.
Map and Set.example: Index jobs by ID with a Map and track seen IDs with a Set.

immutability.definition: Treat existing data as unchanged and create new values when updating it.
immutability.example: Return a new stock object instead of decrementing the input object.

operators and precedence.definition: Operators perform calculations or comparisons. Precedence decides grouping when parentheses are absent.

strings and numbers.definition: Strings represent text; numbers represent numeric values. Their operators and conversions can behave differently.

array map filter reduce sort.definition: map transforms items, filter selects items, reduce combines them, and sort orders them; sort mutates its array.
array map filter reduce sort.example: Count completed jobs with reduce; copy before sorting.

shallow versus deep copy.definition: A shallow copy shares nested references; a deep copy duplicates supported nested data.
shallow versus deep copy.example: Copying stock with spread still shares stock.metadata.

complexity analysis.definition: Describe how time and memory requirements grow with input size, rather than relying only on one timing.
complexity analysis.example: Repeated linear searches may cost more than building an index once.

let const var.definition: let and const are block scoped; var is function scoped. const prevents rebinding, not object mutation.
let const var.example: const stock={available:3} still permits changing stock.available.

scope and hoisting.definition: Scope controls where bindings can be accessed. Bindings are created before execution, but initialization rules differ.
scope and hoisting.example: Reading a let binding before initialization throws a ReferenceError.

closures.definition: A function can retain access to bindings from the scope where it was created.
closures.example: A counter function remembers its private count between calls.

this call bind apply.definition: this depends on invocation for ordinary functions; call/apply supply it, and bind creates a bound function.
this call bind apply.example: Detaching counter.increment can lose the counter receiver.

prototypes and classes.definition: Objects can inherit property lookup through prototypes. Class syntax builds on this object model.
prototypes and classes.example: A class method is normally found on the class prototype.

own properties.definition: Own properties exist directly on an object, rather than being inherited from its prototype.
own properties.example: Object.hasOwn(counter,'count') distinguishes direct state from inherited methods.

ES modules.definition: JavaScript modules use import/export with explicit dependencies and live exported bindings.
ES modules.example: An imported counter binding reflects updates made by its exporting module.

CommonJS.definition: Node's CommonJS module system uses require and module.exports; interoperability depends on runtime rules.
CommonJS.example: A .cjs module exports a normalizeStatus function.

exceptions and finally.definition: throw interrupts normal control flow; catch handles errors; finally runs cleanup when the try block exits.
exceptions and finally.example: A finally block releases a subscription after work throws.

iterables and generators.definition: An iterable produces an iterator; a generator function can yield values lazily and preserve execution state.
iterables and generators.example: jobIds(jobs) yields one ID at a time.

garbage collection.definition: The runtime can reclaim objects that are no longer reachable. Exact collection timing is not guaranteed.
garbage collection.example: A lingering subscription closure can retain an otherwise unused job.

WeakMap and WeakSet.definition: Weak collections reference object keys without keeping them alive solely through that collection; they are not enumerable.
WeakMap and WeakSet.example: Associate private metadata with an object using a WeakMap.

BigInt and Symbol.definition: BigInt represents integers beyond ordinary number precision; Symbol creates unique identity values.

promises.definition: A Promise represents an eventual fulfilled value or rejection; callbacks run after the current synchronous work.
promises.example: searchJobs('pump') returns a Promise of matching jobs.

async await.definition: async returns a Promise; await pauses that function's continuation while other work can proceed.
async await.example: Await a request without treating CPU-heavy loops as nonblocking.

timers.definition: Timers schedule callbacks after a delay threshold; execution can be later when the runtime is busy.
timers.example: A 250 ms debounce timer waits before starting search.

race conditions.definition: An outcome depends on timing or ordering between operations that overlap.
race conditions.example: An old search response arrives after the current query's response.

AbortController.definition: An AbortController sends a cancellation signal to APIs that support it; cancellation remains cooperative.
AbortController.example: Abort an old fetch and separately prevent stale publication.

errors.definition: Errors describe failed operations; programs need a deliberate policy for reporting and recovering from them.
errors.example: A failed current search shows a retryable error.

cleanup.definition: Cleanup releases resources your operation owns when it completes, fails, or is abandoned.
cleanup.example: Clear timers, unsubscribe listeners, and close owned cursors.

event loop.definition: The event loop coordinates execution of scheduled callbacks around synchronous JavaScript work.
event loop.example: A long synchronous report calculation delays other callbacks.

microtasks versus timers.definition: Promise reactions run as microtasks; timer callbacks run through later scheduled tasks. Runtime details still matter.
microtasks versus timers.example: Predict synchronous logging, then a Promise reaction, then a timer.

promise combinators.definition: Promise helpers combine multiple operations with different completion and rejection policies.
promise combinators.example: Compare Promise.all with Promise.allSettled for a batch.

error propagation.definition: A thrown error or rejected Promise must reach a handler that owns the failure policy.
error propagation.example: Await worker results so rejected jobs do not become unhandled failures.

concurrency versus parallelism.definition: Concurrency overlaps progress; parallelism executes work simultaneously. Async I/O does not itself imply multiple CPU threads.
concurrency versus parallelism.example: Three network requests can overlap on one JavaScript thread.

resource cleanup.definition: Cleanup releases resources your operation owns when it completes, fails, or is abandoned.
resource cleanup.example: Clear timers, unsubscribe listeners, and close owned cursors.

type inference.definition: TypeScript often derives a value's type from its expression and context.
type inference.example: A numeric initializer can infer number without an explicit annotation.

interfaces and type aliases.definition: Both describe types; aliases can also name unions and other type expressions.
interfaces and type aliases.example: Use a Job alias for a union of state-specific object types.

optional properties.definition: An optional property may be absent; absence is not always interchangeable with a supplied undefined.
optional properties.example: Distinguish a missing notes field from an explicitly cleared value.

literal types.definition: A literal type allows one exact value rather than every value of its primitive type.
literal types.example: status:'completed' identifies a particular job variant.

unions and intersections.definition: A union accepts one of several shapes; an intersection combines requirements.
unions and intersections.example: Job is a union; a tenant-scoped entity can intersect with {tenantId:string}.

discriminated unions.definition: A union has a shared tag whose value identifies which object shape applies.
discriminated unions.example: status:'completed' narrows the job to a shape with evidence.

narrowing.definition: Checks refine a broad type into a more specific type within a branch.
narrowing.example: Check typeof input === 'number' before numeric operations.

never.definition: never describes a value that cannot occur, useful for unreachable and exhaustive branches.
never.example: An exhaustive status switch assigns its impossible remainder to never.

primitive annotations.definition: TypeScript annotations describe allowed primitive values at compile time.
primitive annotations.example: quantity:number rejects a string in checked TypeScript code.

array and tuple types.definition: An array repeats an element type; a tuple describes specific positions and their types.

enum versus literal union.definition: An enum names related constants; a literal union limits values to specific alternatives.
enum versus literal union.example: 'draft' | 'completed' restricts a job status without an enum object.

generics.definition: Generics parameterize a type or function while preserving relationships between input and output types.
generics.example: Page<Job> retains Job as the item type.

constraints.definition: A generic constraint limits which types a parameter accepts.
constraints.example: K extends keyof T restricts a projection to valid property keys.

keyof.definition: keyof produces the union of a type's property names.
keyof.example: keyof Job can restrict permitted field selections.

indexed access.definition: Indexed access extracts a property or collection element type from another type.
indexed access.example: T[K] describes the selected field's value type.

mapped types.definition: A mapped type transforms properties according to a rule.
mapped types.example: Create a readonly view from every property of a domain object.

conditional types.definition: A conditional type selects a type result based on a type relationship.
conditional types.example: Extract the success value from Result<T,E>.

utility types.definition: Built-in helpers transform types for common needs.

structural typing.definition: Compatibility depends largely on shape rather than a type's declared name.
structural typing.example: Two objects with required id/status fields may be compatible.

readonly.definition: readonly prevents certain mutations through a TypeScript reference; it does not freeze runtime objects.

function types.definition: A function type specifies parameters and return type, including callback contracts.
function types.example: A listener accepts a JobEvent and returns void.

overloads.definition: Overloads describe distinct supported calling shapes while sharing one implementation.
overloads.example: A lookup can accept one ID or an array with matching return contracts.

optional and rest parameters.definition: Optional parameters can be omitted; rest parameters collect a variable number of arguments.
optional and rest parameters.example: A logger accepts an optional context and additional message values.

unknown versus any.definition: unknown requires checking before use; any bypasses many compiler guarantees.
unknown versus any.example: Accept network input as unknown and validate it.

type guards.definition: A predicate or checked condition narrows a type by establishing a property.

runtime schemas.definition: A runtime schema checks actual data shapes; static types alone do not inspect incoming JSON.
runtime schemas.example: Reject a quantity string at the API boundary.

typed errors.definition: Explicit error shapes make failure handling predictable without relying on message text.
typed errors.example: Return {code:'CONFLICT'} for a rejected state transition.

null and undefined.definition: null commonly represents an explicit empty value; undefined often represents absence or an uninitialized result.
null and undefined.example: An API must define whether omitted and null fields differ.

serialization.definition: Serialization converts values into a representation another process or storage can consume.
serialization.example: A worker message must represent its payload safely.

strict compiler options.definition: tsconfig controls compilation and checks; strict options expose unsafe assumptions.
strict compiler options.example: Enable strict and noUncheckedIndexedAccess for missing lookups.

exhaustiveness.definition: Every declared variant must be handled; adding a variant should expose missing decisions.
exhaustiveness.example: Add awaitingApproval and find incomplete status switches.

type-only imports.definition: Type-only imports carry compile-time information and can be removed from emitted JavaScript.
type-only imports.example: import type {Job} avoids treating Job as a runtime value.

module boundaries.definition: Public interfaces separate packages; consumers use exported behavior without depending on a module's internal details.

declaration output.definition: Declaration files publish type information for consumers of compiled packages.

type compatibility.definition: A type is compatible when it can be used safely where another type is expected under compiler rules.
type compatibility.example: A narrowed completed job can be used as a general job.

runtime versus compile-time contracts.definition: Compile-time contracts check source code; runtime contracts check deployed interactions and actual data.
runtime versus compile-time contracts.example: A typed mobile client can still receive malformed JSON.

tsconfig.definition: tsconfig controls compilation and checks; strict options expose unsafe assumptions.
tsconfig.example: Enable strict and noUncheckedIndexedAccess for missing lookups.

source maps.definition: Source maps relate generated code locations to original source for debugging.
source maps.example: Trace a production stack frame back to its TypeScript line.

TypeScript compilation versus execution.definition: TypeScript checks/transforms source; the runtime executes JavaScript and does not automatically enforce annotations.
TypeScript compilation versus execution.example: A compiled API still needs JSON validation.

JSX.definition: JSX describes UI elements using syntax transformed into JavaScript; it is not an HTML string.
JSX.example: Render a JobRow with properties inside a list.

components.definition: Components package UI behavior and presentation into reusable units.
components.example: JobDetails receives a selected job and renders its status.

props.definition: Props are inputs passed from a parent to a component.
props.example: Pass jobId rather than copying unrelated parent state.

composition.definition: Composition builds larger behavior by connecting smaller units through explicit interfaces.
composition.example: A detail view composes a status badge and evidence panel.

events.definition: Events represent user or system actions; handlers decide how state changes.
events.example: A submit handler prevents default navigation and starts assignment.

state.definition: State is stored information that can change and influence behavior or rendering.
state.example: Store selectedJobId and an unsaved notes draft.

reconciliation.definition: Reconciliation resolves differences between local and authoritative state through a defined policy.
reconciliation.example: Present a completion conflict for an authorized decision.

keys.definition: Keys identify siblings across list changes; stable domain IDs avoid mismatched identity.
keys.example: Use job.id rather than a changing array position.

derived state.definition: Derived state can be computed from other inputs instead of separately stored.
derived state.example: Compute selectedJob from selectedJobId and the job list.

immutable updates.definition: Treat existing data as unchanged and create new values when updating it.
immutable updates.example: Return a new stock object instead of decrementing the input object.

Rules of Hooks.definition: Hooks follow stable calling order and permitted call locations so React can associate state correctly.
Rules of Hooks.example: Do not call useState only when a condition is true.

useReducer.definition: useReducer expresses state changes through actions and a reducer function.
useReducer.example: An assignment reducer handles pending, success, and conflict.

Context.definition: Context distributes values through a component tree without passing each intermediate prop.
Context.example: Provide the current organization to nested views.

controlled and uncontrolled inputs.definition: Controlled inputs take their current value from React state; uncontrolled inputs retain it in the host input.
controlled and uncontrolled inputs.example: Choose a controlled notes field for live validation.

form events.definition: Events represent user or system actions; handlers decide how state changes.
form events.example: A submit handler prevents default navigation and starts assignment.

validation.definition: Validation checks incoming data against explicit rules before business code accepts or changes it.

refs.definition: A ref retains a mutable value across renders without its changes causing a render.
refs.example: Keep a timer handle or input reference in useRef.

focus.definition: Focus determines where keyboard input goes; intentional movement makes recovery and navigation usable.
focus.example: Move focus to an invalid field after submission.

routing.definition: Routing selects an endpoint; middleware applies cross-cutting request behavior around handlers.
routing.example: Validate input and attach a request ID before domain work.

URL state.definition: URL state represents shareable navigation/filter values in the address.
URL state.example: Encode selected job and status filter in query parameters.

accessibility.definition: Accessibility makes interactions understandable and usable with different input methods and assistive technology.
accessibility.example: Label controls and support keyboard navigation.

loading and empty states.definition: Loading means data is pending; empty means loading completed without matching data.
loading and empty states.example: Show a loading indicator separately from no matching jobs.

portals.definition: A portal renders UI into another host container while retaining its React relationship.
portals.example: Render an assignment dialog above the main page layout.

focus management.definition: Focus determines where keyboard input goes; intentional movement makes recovery and navigation usable.
focus management.example: Move focus to an invalid field after submission.

useEffect.definition: An effect synchronizes a component with an external system after rendering.
useEffect.example: Subscribe to job updates and return unsubscribe cleanup.

dependency arrays.definition: Effect dependencies describe reactive values used by the effect and when synchronization changes.

useRef.definition: A ref retains a mutable value across renders without its changes causing a render.
useRef.example: Keep a timer handle or input reference in useRef.

custom hooks.definition: A custom hook extracts reusable React behavior while retaining normal hook rules.
custom hooks.example: useJobSubscription owns connection setup and cleanup.

StrictMode.definition: StrictMode adds development checks that expose unsafe behavior, including effect lifecycle problems.
StrictMode.example: A setup-cleanup-setup check reveals a leaked subscription.

render versus commit.definition: Rendering calculates UI; committing applies an accepted result to the host environment.
render versus commit.example: Avoid opening a subscription during render calculation.

component testing.definition: Component testing exercises a UI unit's observable behavior with controlled inputs.
component testing.example: Discuss how an assignment widget should react to rejection.

integration testing.definition: Integration testing exercises connected parts and their boundaries.
integration testing.example: Verify the API and database agree on inventory reservations.

mock boundaries.definition: A mock replaces a dependency; the chosen boundary determines which real behavior is verified.
mock boundaries.example: Control a network response without replacing all UI behavior.

error boundaries.definition: A boundary renders a fallback for supported descendant render/lifecycle failures; it does not catch every async error.
error boundaries.example: Keep navigation working when a detail widget fails.

async event errors.definition: An async event operation can reject outside render-error boundary handling.
async event errors.example: Handle a failed assignment request explicitly.

render errors.definition: Render errors occur while calculating or processing a component's UI.
render errors.example: A broken detail widget throws before it can display.

test isolation.definition: Isolation prevents one verification scenario's state from contaminating another.
test isolation.example: Reset database fixtures between independent scenarios.

server state versus client state.definition: Server state is remote authoritative data; client state includes local interaction and unsaved intent.
server state versus client state.example: Keep a draft separate from the cached confirmed job.

query keys.definition: Query keys identify which remote result is cached and must include relevant inputs.
query keys.example: Include tenant, status, and page in a jobs key.

pagination.definition: Pagination divides a large result into ordered portions with a continuation strategy.
pagination.example: Return jobs with a cursor for the next stable page.

freshness.definition: Freshness describes how current cached data must be for a use case.
freshness.example: A dispatch view may refresh sooner than a historical report.

invalidation.definition: Invalidation marks cached data as outdated after a relevant change.
invalidation.example: Completing a job invalidates affected status lists.

request deduplication.definition: Deduplication shares identical in-flight work rather than issuing redundant requests.
request deduplication.example: Two widgets use one current-job request.

optimistic state.definition: Optimistic state displays expected success before the server confirms, with a recovery policy.
optimistic state.example: Show a technician assignment while its request is pending.

mutation ordering.definition: Mutation ordering decides which overlapping changes may update confirmed or displayed state.
mutation ordering.example: A late first assignment cannot overwrite a newer accepted one.

rollback.definition: Rollback restores a safe earlier application or state version after failure; database reversal requires separate reasoning.
rollback.example: Revert a failed optimistic change without losing newer accepted data.

state machines.definition: A state machine defines allowed states and transitions rather than scattered flags.
state machines.example: A queued operation moves from pending to sending to accepted.

accessible status feedback.definition: Status feedback must be perceivable without depending only on color or sight.
accessible status feedback.example: Announce pending assignment and errors with appropriate semantics.

lazy loading.definition: Lazy loading delays acquiring code or data until it is needed.
lazy loading.example: Load reporting UI only when the reporting route is opened.

Suspense.definition: Suspense coordinates fallback UI for supported suspending work through React/framework integration.
Suspense.example: Show a history fallback while streamed history is pending.

transitions.definition: Transitions mark suitable React updates as lower priority so urgent interaction can proceed.
transitions.example: Keep typing responsive while a large filter result updates.

streaming SSR.definition: Streaming server rendering sends useful HTML progressively rather than waiting for all sections.
streaming SSR.example: Deliver the job summary before slow history finishes.

hydration.definition: Hydration connects client React behavior to existing server-rendered markup.
hydration.example: Match initial server/client content to avoid mismatch.

server/client boundaries.definition: Boundaries decide which work runs on the server and which requires browser interaction.
server/client boundaries.example: Keep credentialed data access on an appropriate server boundary.

framework integration.definition: A framework supplies routing, rendering, and data-loading conventions around React.
framework integration.example: Use supported data loading for a Suspense experiment.

bundle size.definition: Bundle size affects transfer, parsing, and startup cost.
bundle size.example: Measure the initial download before adding a large library.

React Profiler.definition: Profiling measures where time and resources go so changes address actual bottlenecks.
React Profiler.example: Measure row renders before memoizing them.

memoization.definition: Memoization reuses a result when relevant inputs have not changed.
memoization.example: Cache an expensive derived summary when justified.

referential equality.definition: Referential equality compares object identity, not a deep comparison of contents.
referential equality.example: Two separately created {id:1} objects are different references.

context propagation.definition: Changes in a context value can update consumers; placement and identity influence the scope.
context propagation.example: Avoid changing an unrelated global value on every job update.

virtualization.definition: Virtualization renders a visible window of a large collection rather than every item.
virtualization.example: Render only nearby rows in a 10,000-job list.

bundle splitting.definition: Bundle splitting divides code into loadable chunks.
bundle splitting.example: Separate reporting code from the initial dispatch bundle.

memory cleanup.definition: Cleanup releases resources your operation owns when it completes, fails, or is abandoned.
memory cleanup.example: Clear timers, unsubscribe listeners, and close owned cursors.

useMemo versus useCallback.definition: useMemo caches a calculated value; useCallback retains a function identity between relevant changes.
useMemo versus useCallback.example: Stabilize a callback only when its identity affects measured behavior.

native components.definition: Native components map React Native UI descriptions to platform views.
native components.example: Use Text and View rather than browser div elements.

Flexbox.definition: Flexbox lays out items within a container using direction, alignment, and size rules.
Flexbox.example: Arrange technician actions in an adaptive row.

safe areas.definition: Safe areas avoid content being obscured by device cutouts and system UI.
safe areas.example: Keep the completion button above the bottom inset.

navigation.definition: Navigation manages screen transitions and their history.
navigation.example: Open job detail and return to the prior list.

deep links.definition: A deep link routes an external location to a particular application screen.
deep links.example: Open a job from a notification.

keyboard handling.definition: Keyboard handling keeps fields and actions usable when the software keyboard changes available space.
keyboard handling.example: Scroll the focused notes field into view.

platform differences.definition: Android and iOS can differ in permission, layout, navigation, and lifecycle behavior.
platform differences.example: Verify the Android back action separately from iOS navigation.

camera and media permissions.definition: Apps must request and handle platform access to capture or select media.
camera and media permissions.example: Show recovery when camera permission is denied.

local files.definition: Local files have storage locations and lifetimes; temporary files may not be durable evidence.
local files.example: Copy an owned camera result into an appropriate durable location.

local persistence.definition: Persistence stores data beyond the current process's memory.
local persistence.example: Reopen the app and recover completion notes.

app lifecycle.definition: The OS can foreground, background, suspend, or terminate a mobile process.
app lifecycle.example: Persist a draft before claiming it is saved.

async writes.definition: An asynchronous write finishes later; acknowledgement must reflect actual durable completion.
async writes.example: Display saved only after the persistence operation succeeds.

secure versus ordinary storage.definition: Sensitive credentials need protected storage appropriate to the platform; ordinary preferences are not a secret store.
secure versus ordinary storage.example: Keep session credentials out of unencrypted draft storage.

FlatList.definition: FlatList is a React Native component for efficiently presenting scrollable collections.
FlatList.example: Use stable IDs and measure a 5,000-job list.

stable keys.definition: Keys identify siblings across list changes; stable domain IDs avoid mismatched identity.
stable keys.example: Use job.id rather than a changing array position.

gestures.definition: Gestures translate touch movement into interactions with cancellation and conflict rules.
gestures.example: A row swipe opens an action without breaking scrolling.

animations.definition: Animations change visual properties over time and must respect responsiveness and user preferences.
animations.example: Measure a swipe transition under JS load.

JS and UI threads.definition: JavaScript execution and platform UI work have distinct scheduling concerns.
JS and UI threads.example: A JS stall and a UI rendering stall can have different symptoms.

image memory.definition: Decoded image memory can exceed compressed download size.
image memory.example: Resize a large photo for a small thumbnail.

Hermes profiling.definition: Hermes profiling inspects JavaScript work in React Native's JavaScript engine.
Hermes profiling.example: Find CPU-heavy work in a release-build interaction.

native modules.definition: Native modules expose platform functionality through a JavaScript-accessible interface.

typed specifications.definition: A typed native specification describes the interface shared across language boundaries.
typed specifications.example: Declare a native method's parameter and return shapes.

code generation.definition: Code generation produces integration code from a declared interface or schema.
code generation.example: Generate native glue from a module specification.

JSI concepts.definition: JSI is an interface enabling JavaScript and native code to interact; it is not a guarantee of cheap or safe synchronous work.
JSI concepts.example: Explain why a slow native call can still block interaction.

Fabric concepts.definition: Fabric is React Native's renderer architecture that coordinates React and native view work.
Fabric concepts.example: Trace how a changed layout reaches the platform view.

render commit mount.definition: React Native rendering calculates a tree, commits an accepted result, then mounts host changes.
render commit mount.example: Distinguish calculating a row from updating its native view.

threading.definition: Threading determines where work executes and how access is coordinated.
threading.example: Keep expensive work off an interaction-critical thread.

native build tools.definition: Native build tools compile and package platform code and dependencies.
native build tools.example: Use Android tooling and Xcode for platform builds.

HTTP semantics.definition: HTTP methods, status codes, headers, and bodies describe requests and their outcomes.
HTTP semantics.example: Use a stable conflict response for a rejected assignment.

middleware.definition: Routing selects an endpoint; middleware applies cross-cutting request behavior around handlers.
middleware.example: Validate input and attach a request ID before domain work.

request lifecycle.definition: A request passes through admission, handling, response, and cleanup, including disconnects.
request lifecycle.example: Release owned resources if a downloading client leaves.

async errors.definition: A thrown error or rejected Promise must reach a handler that owns the failure policy.
async errors.example: Await worker results so rejected jobs do not become unhandled failures.

configuration.definition: Configuration supplies environment-specific behavior without hardcoding secrets.
configuration.example: Read a database URL from a controlled environment setting.

logging.definition: Logging records diagnostic events with relevant context.
logging.example: Log a request ID and failure category without credentials.

dependency injection.definition: Dependency injection supplies collaborators through interfaces rather than hardcoded global imports.
dependency injection.example: Inject a fake subscription service into an isolated exercise.

ESM.definition: JavaScript modules use import/export with explicit dependencies and live exported bindings.
ESM.example: An imported counter binding reflects updates made by its exporting module.

headers and cookies.definition: Headers carry request/response metadata; cookies can store browser session identifiers with access rules.
headers and cookies.example: Explain HttpOnly and SameSite for a chosen session transport.

JSON parsing limits.definition: Parsing limits bound untrusted body size and complexity before expensive processing.

Buffer.definition: A Buffer represents binary bytes in Node.js.
Buffer.example: Stream attachment chunks rather than treating bytes as a text string.

filesystem promises.definition: Promise-based filesystem APIs provide asynchronous file operations with explicit errors.
filesystem promises.example: Await a file write and handle permission failure.

EventEmitter.definition: EventEmitter lets producers emit named events and listeners subscribe; listener lifetime needs management.
EventEmitter.example: Remove a job listener when its owner is disposed.

package scripts and lockfiles.definition: Scripts name repeatable commands; lockfiles record resolved dependency versions.
package scripts and lockfiles.example: Run a consistent build and install from a committed lockfile.

relational modelling.definition: Relational modelling organizes entities and relationships into constrained tables.
relational modelling.example: Link stock movements to jobs and organizations.

foreign keys.definition: A foreign key constrains a reference to a valid related record.
foreign keys.example: A job assignment must reference an existing technician.

unique and check constraints.definition: Database constraints enforce rules even under concurrent application access.
unique and check constraints.example: Reject duplicate completion keys and negative available stock.

SQL.definition: SQL queries and changes relational data through declared statements.
SQL.example: Select jobs in a stable order within an organization.

indexes.definition: Indexes organize data to accelerate selected access patterns, at a write/storage cost.
indexes.example: Index the tenant and status columns for a common job query.

transactions.definition: A transaction groups changes that commit together or are rolled back.
transactions.example: Complete a job and record inventory movement atomically.

locking.definition: Locks coordinate access when concurrent work would violate a rule.
locking.example: Protect the final stock unit during reservation.

isolation.definition: Isolation determines how concurrent transactions observe and affect one another.
isolation.example: Compare update behavior under competing reservations.

migrations.definition: Migrations change stored schema or data in a controlled, versioned way.
migrations.example: Add approval state without corrupting existing jobs.

query plans.definition: A query plan shows how the database intends to execute a query.
query plans.example: Inspect whether a job list scans all rows or uses an index.

idempotency.definition: An idempotent operation has no extra business effect when repeated according to its contract.
idempotency.example: Retry completion without deducting stock twice.

unique constraints.definition: Database constraints enforce rules even under concurrent application access.
unique constraints.example: Reject duplicate completion keys and negative available stock.

atomicity.definition: Atomicity means grouped changes succeed together or do not take effect.
atomicity.example: Avoid a completed job without its required stock movement.

request fingerprints.definition: A fingerprint identifies the relevant contents of a request for repeat comparison.
request fingerprints.example: Reject the same idempotency key with a different quantity.

concurrent promises.definition: Multiple Promise-producing operations can be in flight at once, requiring bounded admission and error handling.
concurrent promises.example: Limit a batch to three active jobs.

business-state guards.definition: State guards reject operations that are not legal for the current business state.
business-state guards.example: A new key cannot complete an already-completed job twice.

authentication versus authorization.definition: Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides whether that identity may perform an action.
authentication versus authorization.example: A logged-in technician still cannot edit another tenant's job.

sessions versus tokens.definition: Sessions and tokens are ways to carry identity; expiration, storage, and revocation depend on the design.
sessions versus tokens.example: Define how a revoked mobile session stops queued commands.

password hashing when applicable.definition: Password hashing stores a one-way, deliberately expensive verifier instead of a recoverable password.
password hashing when applicable.example: Use a suitable maintained password-hashing implementation if passwords are supported.

RBAC and resource rules.definition: Role permissions describe categories of actions; resource rules check the particular object's ownership or assignment.
RBAC and resource rules.example: Technician role alone does not permit changing every job.

tenant isolation.definition: Tenant isolation prevents one organization's data from leaking into another's operations.
tenant isolation.example: Scope API queries, files, caches, and subscriptions by organization.

CSRF and CORS.definition: CSRF abuses ambient credentials for unwanted actions; CORS controls browser cross-origin response access, not API authorization.
CSRF and CORS.example: Choose relevant protections for cookie-based mutation requests.

rate limiting.definition: Rate limiting bounds how often callers can consume a service.
rate limiting.example: Limit abusive upload or login traffic with a documented response.

TLS basics.definition: TLS protects transport confidentiality and integrity and authenticates endpoints through certificate validation.
TLS basics.example: Use validated HTTPS for mobile API calls.

HTTP security headers.definition: Security headers tell browsers about content, framing, transport, and related restrictions.
HTTP security headers.example: Choose content and framing policies for the web shell.

local transactions.definition: Local transactions commit related offline records together.
local transactions.example: Store an operation and its draft update consistently.

durability.definition: Durability means acknowledged data survives the failures covered by the storage contract.
durability.example: A saved draft survives process termination.

local database migrations.definition: Local migrations evolve device storage while preserving supported old data.
local database migrations.example: Upgrade a queued v1 command record.

retry and backoff.definition: Retry transient failures with increasing delays and a bounded stopping policy.
retry and backoff.example: Retry an upload after a temporary timeout, not a validation error.

jitter.definition: Jitter adds randomized delay so many clients do not retry at the same instant.
jitter.example: Spread reconnect retries after a network outage.

per-entity ordering.definition: Ordering is preserved for operations that depend on the same entity while independent entities can proceed.
per-entity ordering.example: A job start must not overtake its earlier assignment.

batching.definition: Batching combines work to reduce overhead while preserving limits and error visibility.
batching.example: Send bounded groups of queued changes after reconnect.

cancellation.definition: Cancellation defines how unfinished work stops and how owned resources are released.
cancellation.example: Disposed search must not publish a later response.

connectivity signals.definition: A device connection signal is a hint, not proof that a particular service is reachable.
connectivity signals.example: Handle API failure even when the phone reports Wi-Fi.

optimistic concurrency.definition: An operation checks that the stored version still matches the version it edited.
optimistic concurrency.example: Reject completion based on an outdated cancelled-job version.

versions.definition: Versions identify revisions of data or contracts so changes can be detected and negotiated.
versions.example: Include a job revision with an edit.

conflict detection.definition: Conflict detection recognizes incompatible concurrent intent rather than silently overwriting it.
conflict detection.example: Notice offline completion against online cancellation.

domain policy.definition: Domain policy states the business decision when several technically possible behaviors exist.
domain policy.example: Decide whether cancellation requires reviewing captured evidence.

audit history.definition: An audit history preserves attributable changes and decisions for investigation.
audit history.example: Retain the cancellation and attempted completion.

clock skew.definition: Clock skew means device timestamps can disagree and cannot alone prove global order.
clock skew.example: Do not choose a conflict winner solely by phone time.

chunking.definition: Chunking divides a large payload into manageable pieces.
chunking.example: Send a large photo archive in resumable chunks.

checksums.definition: A checksum summarizes content so unexpected changes can be detected under its stated guarantees.
checksums.example: Verify uploaded chunks and the assembled file.

resumability.definition: Resumability continues from a durable checkpoint after interruption.
resumability.example: Restart an upload from accepted chunks.

file streams.definition: Streams process data incrementally instead of loading the entire payload at once.
file streams.example: Stream report rows or attachment bytes.

resource lifecycle.definition: A resource has creation, ownership, use, completion, and cleanup rules.
resource lifecycle.example: A partial upload expires and its temporary chunks are removed.

upload authorization.definition: Upload authorization checks who may create, continue, and attach a file to a resource.
upload authorization.example: Revalidate ownership before accepting a resumed chunk.

mobile background limits.definition: The OS can limit or stop background execution; clients must not rely on uninterrupted work.
mobile background limits.example: Resume a persisted upload after the app restarts.

SSE versus WebSockets.definition: SSE sends a server-to-client event stream; WebSockets provide a bidirectional connection with different protocol needs.
SSE versus WebSockets.example: Choose a transport for live dispatch updates.

ordering.definition: Ordering defines which sequence guarantees consumers can rely on.
ordering.example: Specify whether job events are ordered per job or globally.

cursors.definition: A cursor identifies a continuation position in results or event history.
cursors.example: Resume updates after the last processed event.

deduplication.definition: Deduplication recognizes repeated work or events and avoids repeated effects.

reconnect.definition: Reconnect restores a broken connection and may require application-state recovery.
reconnect.example: Reconnect and replay missed updates before marking the board current.

authentication.definition: Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides whether that identity may perform an action.
authentication.example: A logged-in technician still cannot edit another tenant's job.

snapshot plus event stream.definition: A snapshot gives current state; an event stream carries changes. Their boundary must avoid a gap.
snapshot plus event stream.example: Fetch a snapshot with a compatible stream cursor.

transactional outbox.definition: An outbox stores side-effect intent in the same database transaction as the business change.
transactional outbox.example: Commit completion and its notification intent together.

at-least-once processing.definition: At-least-once processing can repeat deliveries, so consumers must tolerate duplicates.
at-least-once processing.example: A worker crash causes a notification attempt to be retried.

idempotent consumers.definition: An idempotent consumer prevents duplicate deliveries from repeating a business effect.
idempotent consumers.example: Record a processed operation ID before repeating a stock adjustment.

queues.definition: Queues buffer work for later consumers and need admission, capacity, and failure policies.
queues.example: Hold notification jobs while the provider is unavailable.

dead letters.definition: Dead letters retain work that cannot be processed normally for inspection or recovery.

retry budgets.definition: A retry budget bounds attempts or time to avoid endless overload.
retry budgets.example: Stop automatic retries after a defined limit and surface the failure.

distributed transactions.definition: Distributed transactions coordinate changes across multiple systems; simpler local transactions do not cover remote effects.
distributed transactions.example: A database commit cannot atomically guarantee a third-party notification.

Node streams.definition: Streams process data incrementally instead of loading the entire payload at once.
Node streams.example: Stream report rows or attachment bytes.

backpressure.definition: Backpressure slows a producer when its consumer cannot keep up.
backpressure.example: A slow download prevents unbounded report buffering.

pipeline.definition: A pipeline connects processing stages with error and cleanup coordination.
pipeline.example: Pipe generated rows through CSV formatting to a response.

async iterators.definition: Async iterators yield values over time through an asynchronous iteration protocol.
async iterators.example: Read report rows using for await.

buffering.definition: Buffering temporarily accumulates data; uncontrolled buffering can exhaust memory.
buffering.example: Limit queued chunks between a database cursor and client.

database cursors.definition: A database cursor incrementally reads query results while owning database resources.
database cursors.example: Close the cursor when the downloading client disconnects.

CSV correctness.definition: CSV output needs proper quoting, line handling, encoding, and a policy for spreadsheet interpretation.
CSV correctness.example: Escape a comma-containing note and handle formula-leading text.

event-loop delay.definition: Event-loop delay measures how long scheduled JS work is delayed by runtime load.
event-loop delay.example: Compare API responsiveness during a synchronous calculation.

worker_threads.definition: Worker threads run JavaScript in separate execution contexts for suitable CPU work.
worker_threads.example: Offload a scheduling simulation to a bounded pool.

pool sizing.definition: Pool sizing balances concurrency against CPU, memory, and queue overhead.
pool sizing.example: Too many CPU workers can reduce useful throughput.

CPU versus I/O.definition: CPU work calculates; I/O waits for external resources. They require different scaling strategies.
CPU versus I/O.example: A report calculation and a database wait are different bottlenecks.

message serialization.definition: Serialization converts values into a representation another process or storage can consume.
message serialization.example: A worker message must represent its payload safely.

signals.definition: Process signals notify software about lifecycle or other operating-system events.
signals.example: Handle termination by stopping admission and draining accepted work.

graceful shutdown.definition: Graceful shutdown stops new work and safely finishes or persists accepted work before exiting.
graceful shutdown.example: Do not lose acknowledged worker jobs during deployment.

timeouts.definition: A timeout bounds waiting but may leave an uncertain outcome if work committed elsewhere.
timeouts.example: A timed-out completion might still have succeeded.

micro frontends versus modules.definition: Micro frontends compose separately built web features; modules can share one build and release.

build-time versus runtime integration.definition: Build-time integration bundles features together; runtime integration loads or connects separately built features during execution.

ownership.definition: Ownership identifies who maintains a feature, its public contracts and its recovery behavior.

coupling.definition: Coupling is how strongly one component depends on another; stronger dependencies make independent change harder.

shared dependencies.definition: Shared dependencies are libraries used by multiple features; their versions and runtime instances must remain compatible.

architecture decisions.definition: An architecture decision explains a system choice, alternatives, evidence and consequences for future change.

module federation or equivalent.definition: Module Federation lets separately built applications share code at runtime; alternatives must meet the same integration requirements.

runtime manifests.definition: A runtime manifest tells the shell which feature version to load and where its artifact is located.

shared React identity.definition: The shell and remotes must use compatible React runtime instances so component and Hook behavior remains valid.

bundler configuration.definition: Bundler settings determine how source code becomes executable artifacts, including imports, chunks and shared libraries.

CSS isolation.definition: CSS isolation prevents a feature's styles from accidentally changing another feature's interface.

event contracts.definition: An event contract defines a message's name, payload, version and meaning for producers and consumers.

schema validation.definition: A runtime schema checks actual data shapes; static types alone do not inspect incoming JSON.
schema validation.example: Reject a quantity string at the API boundary.

version negotiation.definition: Version negotiation selects a contract version both communicating components can understand.

cache invalidation.definition: Invalidation marks cached data as outdated after a relevant change.
cache invalidation.example: Completing a job invalidates affected status lists.

rollbacks.definition: Rollback restores a safe earlier application or state version after failure; database reversal requires separate reasoning.
rollbacks.example: Revert a failed optimistic change without losing newer accepted data.

contract tests.definition: Contract tests check whether a producer and consumer agree on their shared inputs, outputs and errors.

package boundaries.definition: Package boundaries define public imports and prevent consumers from relying on private implementation details.

dependency graphs.definition: A dependency graph shows which packages rely on others; cycles and hidden dependencies make change harder.

navigation contracts.definition: Navigation contracts define route names, parameters and expected destination behavior across mobile features.

shared domain code.definition: Shared domain code contains platform-independent business rules reused by web, mobile and server features.

native build compatibility.definition: Native build compatibility means feature code and native dependencies work with the application's platform toolchain and binary.

mobile release constraints.definition: Mobile changes must respect native binary compatibility, platform requirements and the chosen release/update mechanism.

threat modelling.definition: Threat modelling identifies assets, possible attackers and abuse paths so protections address actual product risks.

secure storage.definition: Sensitive credentials need protected storage appropriate to the platform; ordinary preferences are not a secret store.
secure storage.example: Keep session credentials out of unencrypted draft storage.

input and upload limits.definition: Size, count and format limits bound incoming data so requests cannot exhaust resources or bypass rules.

content validation.definition: Content validation inspects the actual data or file, rather than trusting its name or declared type.

credential lifecycle.definition: Credential lifecycle covers creation, storage, use, rotation, expiry and revocation of secrets or access credentials.

CSRF CORS CSP.definition: CSRF protects authenticated actions, CORS governs browser cross-origin access, and CSP limits allowed content execution.
CSRF CORS CSP.example: Apply the controls relevant to the deployed browser architecture.

least privilege.definition: Least privilege grants only the permissions needed for a person, service or database operation.

dependency security.definition: Dependency security examines third-party packages, known vulnerabilities and update risks in the application's dependencies.

load models.definition: A load model describes realistic request rates, users and workloads for a performance measurement.

percentiles.definition: A percentile describes how much of a measured distribution falls below a value; p95 latency includes 95 percent of requests.

profiling.definition: Profiling measures where time and resources go so changes address actual bottlenecks.
profiling.example: Measure row renders before memoizing them.

database plans.definition: A query plan shows how the database intends to execute a query.
database plans.example: Inspect whether a job list scans all rows or uses an index.

network cost.definition: Network cost includes transferred bytes, request overhead and delay between the client and server.

memory leaks.definition: A memory leak retains data that is no longer needed, increasing memory use as the application runs.

capacity and cost.definition: Capacity and cost relate required throughput, resource limits and operating expense under a defined workload.

structured logging.definition: Structured logging records consistent named fields so events can be searched and compared reliably.

metrics.definition: Metrics are numeric measurements over time, such as request count, latency or queue depth.

tracing.definition: Tracing connects the steps of one operation across components to show where time or failure occurred.

AsyncLocalStorage.definition: Node's AsyncLocalStorage associates context with an asynchronous operation, such as its request or correlation ID.

SLIs and SLOs.definition: A service-level indicator measures behavior; a service-level objective sets a target for that measurement.

alert design.definition: Alert design identifies a meaningful failure condition, threshold and response without generating unnecessary noise.

privacy.definition: Privacy limits collection, use and exposure of personal or sensitive data, including logs and reports.

CI/CD.definition: Continuous integration validates changes; continuous delivery or deployment prepares or releases reproducible application artifacts.

artifact reproducibility.definition: Artifact reproducibility means the same declared source, dependencies and build settings produce a repeatable release.

migration safety.definition: Migration safety preserves valid data and compatible clients while changing database structures or stored values.

backups.definition: A backup is a preserved copy of data that can be used to recover from loss or corruption.

restore verification.definition: Restore verification checks recovered data and business behavior; possessing a backup alone does not prove recovery works.

recovery objectives.definition: Recovery objectives specify acceptable data loss and acceptable time to restore a working service.

unit versus integration versus end-to-en.definition: Unit checks isolate a small behavior; integration checks connected parts; end-to-end checks exercise a complete user workflow.

property-based testing.definition: Property-based testing generates varied inputs and checks general rules, such as stock never becoming negative.

API compatibility.definition: API compatibility keeps existing clients working when request, response or business behavior changes.

domain migrations.definition: Migrations change stored schema or data in a controlled, versioned way.
domain migrations.example: Add approval state without corrupting existing jobs.

local migrations.definition: Local migrations evolve device storage while preserving supported old data.
local migrations.example: Upgrade a queued v1 command record.

feature negotiation.definition: Feature negotiation determines which capabilities a client and server both support before using them.

deprecation.definition: Deprecation announces that a capability will be retired and gives consumers a supported transition path.

contract testing.definition: Contract testing verifies producer and consumer agreement at a versioned boundary.

domain invariants.definition: Domain invariants are business rules that must remain true, such as accepted consumption never exceeding available stock.

state transitions.definition: A state transition changes an entity from one valid state to another according to business rules.

compensating actions.definition: A compensating action creates a new business operation to correct an accepted effect while preserving its history.

UX.definition: User experience includes how clearly a person can understand, complete and recover from a product workflow.

audit trails.definition: An audit history preserves attributable changes and decisions for investigation.
audit trails.example: Retain the cancellation and attempted completion.

cross-platform contracts.definition: Cross-platform contracts preserve business meaning across web, mobile and server implementations.

debugging.definition: Debugging uses observations and controlled experiments to identify the cause of incorrect behavior.

distributed failure.definition: Distributed failure occurs when connected components fail or disagree independently, including partial success and lost responses.

observability.definition: Observability uses logs, metrics and traces to understand a system's internal behavior from its outputs.

hypothesis testing.definition: In debugging, hypothesis testing proposes a cause, predicts evidence and runs an experiment to confirm or reject it.

regression testing.definition: Regression testing checks that a change has not broken behavior that previously worked.

incident communication.definition: Incident communication describes the observed impact, evidence, response and recovery status clearly to the relevant people.

architecture tradeoffs.definition: Architecture tradeoffs compare the benefits and costs of a design under the product's actual constraints.

system boundaries.definition: System boundaries identify responsibilities and interfaces between components, including where failures and trust assumptions change.

cost.definition: Cost includes implementation effort, operating resources, maintenance burden and the effect of failure.

communication.definition: Communication expresses a problem, evidence, decision and expected behavior clearly enough for others to act.

fundamental recall.definition: Fundamental recall means explaining and applying basic concepts again without relying on memorized recipes.

knowledge transfer.definition: Knowledge transfer enables another person to understand and apply a concept, while checking their independent reasoning.
